prompt.context: Our client, High Q Plastics, is an automotive parts supplier in the U.S. They primarily manufacture and sell plastic injection-molded parts, such as grills, door handles, and decorative trim, to automotive customers. The client has two primary revenue sources: large automotive OEMs and aftermarket. The client has recently seen declining profits, primarily due to increased price competition from new overseas competitors in China. Annual profits have declined from $50M to $20M over the past few years.
prompt.question: What is the reason behind declining profitability? How can High Q improve profits? Can they reach $100M in profits by 2014?

clarifying_info.q: What is the trend in overall automotive sales?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive sales overall are still growing steadily, driven by emerging markets.
Automotive manufacturing is leaving the U.S.

clarifying_info.q: Where does High Q stand relative to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: High Q is currently one of the leaders in this category.

clarifying_info.q: Where is High Q's manufacturing based?
How have High Q's revenues trended?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues have been slowly declining over the last 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: How does High Q's product quality compare to Chinese competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client's products are of higher quality than most Chinese competitors' products.

clarifying_info.q: Why are OEM customers putting pressure on prices?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive OEM customers are looking to reduce cost, driving increased price competition among parts suppliers.

exhibits.title: High Q's 2010 Financials, By Facility
exhibits.shows: A table showing 2010 revenues, labor costs, material costs, overhead costs, and net profits for each of High Q's four U.S. plants (Plant A, B, C, D).

exhibits.title: 2010 U.S. Automotive Market
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing 2010 U.S. automotive sales split by vehicle type, with a note on total market size.

exhibits.title: U.S. Automotive OEM Market — Truck/SUV Market Share 2010 vs. 2014
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart showing 2010 and 2014 predicted OEM market share in the Truck & SUV segment for Ford, GM, Chrysler, Toyota, and Nissan, plus a note on High Q's relationship with Toyota.

data.Additional Info: High Q supplies 70% of Toyota's business; Avg. price of High Q products sold to Toyota = $20

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; decompose each side
Revenue: volume trends (OEM vs. aftermarket), pricing pressure, product mix
Costs: labor costs, raw material costs, overhead/fixed costs, SG&A
Competitive dynamics: who are the new Chinese competitors, what is their cost and quality advantage
Customer mix: OEM vs. aftermarket profitability comparison
Geographic/operational footprint: plant efficiency, proximity to customers

questions.prompt: What key questions would you ask an industry expert to understand the reasons behind High Q's declining profits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply a MECE framework across four areas: (a) Industry — sales volume trends, OEM vs. aftermarket segment growth and profitability; (b) Competitors — relative market share, pricing vs. High Q, cost structure comparison, quality or technology advantages; (c) Revenue — how High Q's prices have changed and whether declines are across all customers/products; (d) Costs — trends in labor and material costs for High Q.

questions.prompt: The CEO of High Q wants to know if $100M in annual profits is achievable by 2014. What would you need to know in order to determine this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the key profit drivers: annual quantity of units sold (Q), selling price (P), variable costs (VC), and fixed costs (FC). The profit formula is Profit = Q*(P - VC) - FC. Candidate should request data on each of these components by plant, product line, and customer segment.

steps: Identify Q (volume), P (price), VC (variable cost per unit), FC (fixed costs)
Note current profits = $20M; target = $100M; gap = $80M increase needed
math.answer: $100M target requires identifying specific levers across volume, price, and cost to close an $80M gap from current $20M

questions.prompt: What ways can you think of to increase revenues? What ways can you think of to reduce costs?
questions.guidance: Revenue ideas: segment customers to identify price sensitivity, increase marketing/presence in the aftermarket segment (less price-competitive), negotiate long-term contracts with OEM customers to lock in volume. Cost reduction ideas: find alternative/cheaper raw material sources, invest in process automation to reduce labor costs, consolidate manufacturing sites (especially high-overhead plants) to reduce SG&A, relocate plants closer to customers to reduce transportation costs.

questions.prompt: The client plans to implement lean manufacturing across all 4 U.S. plants. The client expects to produce 80% of 2010 volumes in 2014 and plans to reduce prices by 10% due to competition. Lean manufacturing will provide an additional 20% savings in raw materials and 30% savings in labor. What is the change in profits from 2010 to 2014?
questions.guidance: Work through each plant: (1) Revenues fall to 80% of 2010 then an additional 10% price reduction => 80% * 90% = 72% of 2010 revenue; (2) Labor falls to 80% of 2010 (volume) then 30% further => 80% * 70% = 56% of 2010 labor; (3) Material falls to 80% of 2010 (volume) then 20% further => 80% * 80% = 64% of 2010 material; (4) Overhead stays flat. Candidate should note total 2014 profits = $28M vs. 2010 profits = $20M, an improvement of $8M, far short of the $100M goal.

math.setup: For each plant: 2014 Revenue = 2010 Revenue * 0.8 * 0.9; 2014 Labor = 2010 Labor * 0.8 * 0.7; 2014 Material = 2010 Material * 0.8 * 0.8; 2014 Overhead = 2010 Overhead (unchanged)
math.answer: Total 2014 profits = $28M; profit improvement = $8M. The $100M target is not achievable under this plan alone.

questions.prompt: High Q's CEO asks you to analyze Toyota's predicted 30% increase in truck and SUV market share. Based on Exhibits 2 and 3, what additional profits can High Q expect from this?
questions.guidance: Use Exhibit 2 to calculate 2010 truck & SUV sales volume, then use Exhibit 3 market share figures to derive Toyota's 2010 and 2014 volumes. Apply High Q's 70% supply share and $20 avg price to get revenues, then compute the incremental revenue. Candidate should note that the question asks for additional profits — since the question only provides revenue data without a margin figure, presenting additional revenue ($13.44M) as a proxy is acceptable. Rounded answers of $13M or $14M are acceptable.

math.setup: U.S. Auto Market 2010 = 16M vehicles; Trucks & SUVs = 20% of market; Toyota Truck/SUV share: 10% in 2010, 40% in 2014; High Q supplies 70% of Toyota; Avg price = $20/unit
steps: High Q Qty Sold to Toyota 2010 = 320,000 * 70% = 224,000
High Q Qty Sold to Toyota 2014 = 1,280,000 * 70% = 896,000
math.answer: Additional revenue from Toyota growth = ~$13.4M (rounded $13M-$14M is acceptable)

brainstorming.prompt: What ways can you think of to increase revenues and reduce costs for High Q Plastics?

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Find alternative raw material sources to reduce material costs
Invest in process automation to reduce labor costs
Consolidate multiple U.S. manufacturing plants (especially Plant D with high overhead) to reduce SG&A
Relocate manufacturing closer to customers to reduce transportation costs
Implement lean manufacturing to reduce waste across all plants

categories.name: Revenue Growth
ideas: Segment OEM customers to identify those with lower price sensitivity and protect margins
Increase marketing and sales effort in the aftermarket segment, which may be less price-competitive
Negotiate long-term supply contracts with OEM customers to lock in volume
Leverage quality advantage vs. Chinese competitors to justify premium pricing with quality-conscious OEMs
Pursue Toyota relationship growth given Toyota's rising U.S. truck/SUV market share
Diversify into plastic injection-molded parts for non-automotive industries to reduce dependence on price-pressured auto OEMs

recommendation: High Q should proceed with the lean manufacturing implementation across all four plants, as it improves annual profits from $20M to $28M
However, lean manufacturing alone is insufficient to reach the CEO's $100M profit target by 2014 — the CEO's expectations need to be recalibrated
risks: Continued price competition from Chinese manufacturers could erode gains from lean manufacturing
Reduced volumes (80% of 2010) may underutilize plant capacity and increase per-unit overhead
Plant D's high overhead structure remains a drag on profitability even post-lean
next_steps: Evaluate consolidation of the four U.S. plants, prioritizing closure or restructuring of Plant D given its disproportionately high overhead
Develop a dedicated growth strategy for the aftermarket segment, which is likely less exposed to OEM price pressure
Explore diversification into plastic injection-molded parts for non-automotive industries (e.g., consumer goods, industrial equipment) to reduce concentration risk
Capitalize on Toyota's rising truck/SUV market share — High Q's existing 70% supply relationship positions it well for incremental volume growth
